analysis.one_liner: Caps carbon emissions from oil, coal, and gas and pays every household an equal dividend from the auction proceeds.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a single cosponsor; it sat in two House committees until the two-year Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required oil refineries, coal mines, and natural gas suppliers to buy a shrinking number of carbon permits at auction, cutting emissions 80% below 2005 levels by 2040. Every dollar raised would have been mailed back as an equal quarterly dividend to each person lawfully in the United States. Because the dividend is the same for everyone, households that use less energy than average — most low- and middle-income families — would come out ahead. It also would have imposed fees on carbon-intensive imports from countries without comparable climate rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Every eligible U.S. resident lawfully present with a valid Social Security number would receive the same quarterly, tax-free dividend, funded entirely by permit auction proceeds and penalties [S3]. Since the payment is identical per person, households whose energy use is below average — most low- and middle-income families, renters, and city dwellers — would receive more than they pay in higher fuel prices [S3]. Everyone also gains from a declining emissions cap that reaches 80% below 2005 levels by 2040, and from cleaner air [S2]. U.S. steel, cement, and other energy-intensive manufacturers would be shielded from foreign competition by fees on carbon-intensive imports and rebates for exports [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every U.S. household, via equal dividends

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Healthy Climate Trust Fund that turns 100% of carbon permit auction revenue and penalties into an equal quarterly, tax-free dividend for every eligible person lawfully present in the United States — no means test, no phase-out for higher earners

Because the dividend is identical per person, households with below-average energy use — most low- and middle-income families — would collect more than the added cost passed through fuel prices, making the program net-progressive
Sets a hard, declining cap on carbon permits that falls to 80% below 2005 emission levels by 2040, with interim targets of 50% below by 2030

Imposes carbon-equivalency fees on imports of steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper, and chemicals from countries without comparable climate rules, and pays equivalent rebates to U.S. exporters, so domestic manufacturers are not undercut and pollution does not simply move overseas

States that carbon permits are not property rights and restricts trading to covered fuel companies with anti-speculation holding limits, preventing Wall Street from turning the permits into a speculative asset
Requires the EPA to regulate all other greenhouse gases — outside the covered fuels — within 10 years, and preserves citizens' ability to sue to enforce that duty

analysis.who_pays: Oil refineries and petroleum importers, coal mines, and natural gas suppliers would have to buy a permit for every ton of carbon their fuels emit, and they would pass those costs into gasoline, heating, and electricity prices [S3]. Consumers — especially drivers, rural households, and people with long commutes and high heating bills — would pay more for energy, and only see that money back when the dividend arrives. Fossil fuel workers and coal communities would bear job losses as production shrinks, and the bill contains no dedicated transition assistance for them. The program would also cost Treasury and EPA administrative resources, though the trust fund covers its own costs [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers

drawbacks.text: Fuel, electricity, and heating costs would rise for every household immediately, while dividends are paid quarterly and in arrears — a timing gap that hits cash-strapped families first; high-energy-use households (rural drivers, large homes, cold climates) could pay more than they ever receive

The bill provides no transition assistance for coal miners, oil and gas workers, or the communities built around those industries, even though the permit cap steadily shrinks their market to near zero by 2040

Its own findings cite the IPCC's call for emissions 45% below 2010 levels by 2030, yet the bill's schedule (50% below 2005 by 2030) is slower than that benchmark, and an emergency provision merely requires the Treasury Secretary to report to Congress rather than act
Greenhouse gases from producing animals for food are exempted from regulation, leaving agricultural emissions — a major U.S. source of methane — untouched
The Secretary can borrow permits from future years and release reserve permits to stabilize prices, which weakens the emissions guarantee in any year when prices spike

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is unusually favorable to ordinary households: 100% of the money goes back as equal dividends, so most low- and middle-income families would net a gain, and the anti-speculation and border-adjustment provisions close the usual loopholes in cap-and-trade schemes. The honest costs are real but manageable in principle: higher energy prices concentrated on high-consumption households, and severe dislocation in coal and oil regions with no worker assistance in the bill. The bigger shortcoming is ambition — the emission schedule lags the IPCC benchmark the bill itself cites, and agricultural emissions are exempt. On balance this is a well-built, worker-unfriendly-in-one-spot but household-friendly climate bill that never got a chance to be tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, bounced to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer introduced the bill on March 28, 2019; it was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee
The next day it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change, a step beneath full-committee consideration
Not one member of the House — of either party — signed on as a cosponsor during the entire two years the bill was alive
Neither committee ever held a hearing or markup, no floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and their supply chains came out ahead: no carbon permits were ever required, and no carbon price touched oil, coal, or natural gas. U.S. manufacturers of carbon-intensive goods also avoided adjusting to a carbon fee, and the status quo of no federal climate pricing continued.

for.name: Rep. Don Beyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in the House for its entire two-year life

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (Chair Frank Pallone, D)
against.what_they_did: Held no hearing or markup on the bill in two years; its Environment and Climate Change subcommittee took no recorded action after referral

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral (Chair Richard Neal, D)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — on the bill's tax and dividend provisions before the Congress ended

against.name: All 434 other House members
against.what_they_did: Not a single one — Democrat, Republican, or Independent — cosigned the bill across two years, leaving it with no coalition to push committee leadership

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split can be measured; the sponsor was a Democrat and zero of the other 230 House Democrats and 197 House Republicans cosponsored [S4].

industries.note: Coal mines and coal importers would buy a permit for every ton of carbon their fuel emits, and coal is the most carbon-intensive covered fuel, so the cap squeezes it hardest. The industry's avoidance of that cost came at the price of continued carbon emissions the public pays for in climate damage and air pollution.

Refineries and petroleum product importers would face permit costs on crude oil and derived fuels, passed into gasoline and diesel prices. Their interest in the bill's failure ran directly against the dividend payments ordinary households would have received from those same fees.

Gas suppliers and processors would buy permits on every ton of CO2 from delivered gas, raising heating and power costs. Avoiding the permit requirement preserved their cost position against cleaner competitors.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper, chemicals)
industries.note: They would absorb higher energy costs embedded in fuel prices, but the bill's border fees on carbon-intensive imports and rebates for exports were designed to leave them whole against foreign competition. Their stake in the bill was genuinely two-sided.

A shrinking carbon cap makes fossil fuels progressively more expensive relative to wind, solar, and efficiency, accelerating the market shift toward cleaner sources. The public's interest in emissions cuts and this industry's growth run together here.

The bill bars anyone but covered fuel companies from buying permits and directs the Treasury to set holding limits to prevent speculation, hoarding, and manipulation. Wall Street was excluded from a market it has profited from in past cap-and-trade designs, which protects the dividends households were meant to receive.
